item.prompt: In an argumentative essay, where does the thesis statement usually appear?
options: At the end of the introduction
In the middle of the second body paragraph
item.hint: Think about what the reader needs to know before the body paragraphs begin.
item.workedExample: The thesis ends the introduction so the reader knows the claim and reasons before the body paragraphs argue them.

item.prompt: Which sentence is an arguable thesis statement?
options: Our school should start a debate club because debating builds confidence and clear thinking.
This essay is about debate clubs.
item.hint: Could a sensible person disagree with it?
item.workedExample: Only the debate-club claim can be argued, and it names two reasons. The others are a fact, an announcement and a topic.

item.prompt: Reason: reading every day builds vocabulary. Which evidence supports this reason best? (Musu's school is the made-up practice school from the lesson.)
options: Musu's class read for 20 minutes a day for one term, and many learners then used new words from the books in their own writing.
item.hint: Which option is specific and proves this exact reason?
item.workedExample: The example from Musu's class is specific and shows vocabulary growing. The others are opinions or unrelated facts. In real writing, the example must come from a real class or a source you can name.

item.prompt: What should the conclusion of an argumentative essay do?
options: Introduce a new reason the reader has not seen
Restate the thesis in new words and sum up the main reasons
Repeat the introduction word for word
item.hint: Remember the three jobs of a conclusion.
item.workedExample: A conclusion restates the thesis in new words, sums up the reasons and ends with a final thought. New reasons belong in the body.

item.prompt: In a PEEL paragraph, what does the Explain sentence do?
options: It shows how the evidence supports the point
It repeats the evidence word for word
item.hint: The Explain sentence answers: so what?
item.workedExample: Explain connects the evidence to the point, showing why the evidence proves it.

options: Some people say a debate club takes time from homework, but meetings can be held once a week after classes.
item.hint: Look for an objection followed by a reply.
item.workedExample: It states an objection (time from homework) and answers it (meet once a week), which is how an essay answers the other side.

writingRubric.use: Candidate rubric, teacher-scored: formative feedback on in-lesson writing, and the proposed scoring guide for the candidate end-of-lesson writing tasks (assessment definitions). Nothing in the platform computes a score or mastery from it; Assessment Player V2 has no constructed-response item type, and it becomes mastery evidence only after qualified review and a governed release.

criteria.label: Thesis statement
criteria.secure: An arguable claim that names two clear reasons.
criteria.developing: A claim with one reason, or reasons that are vague.
criteria.beginning: A topic, a fact or an announcement instead of a claim.

criteria.label: Point (topic sentence)
criteria.secure: States reason one clearly and matches the thesis.
criteria.developing: States a reason that only loosely matches the thesis.
criteria.beginning: No topic sentence, or it repeats the thesis word for word.

criteria.label: Evidence
criteria.secure: Specific, true and relevant evidence (example, checkable fact or experience).
criteria.beginning: Opinion, an invented figure, or unrelated evidence.

criteria.label: Explain and link
criteria.secure: Explains how the evidence proves the point and links back to the claim.
criteria.developing: Explains or links, but not both; or the Explain sentence only restates the evidence.

criteria.label: Counterargument and reply
criteria.secure: States a fair objection and answers it with a reason.
criteria.developing: States an objection but the reply only repeats the claim.
criteria.beginning: No objection, or an objection left unanswered.

assessmentDefinitions.notice: Candidate assessment definitions for the v0.3.0 lesson (Curriculum Excellence Standard V1). Unreviewed and unreleased: nothing scores them, writes mastery from them or releases them. Writing is teacher-scored with the candidate rubric until a qualified reviewer approves it and a governed release binds it. Scoring guides are reviewer only and must never reach a learner projection, offline package or client bundle.
assessmentDefinitions.diagnosticOnlyRationale: These three exit items test recall of where essay parts go and what they do. They stay in the exit ticket to show the teacher which idea to revisit, but they are not mastery evidence: pl-w1, pl-r1 and pl-r2 test the same knowledge by use. If released, they must be configured as non-mastery items.

tasks.prompt: Write a short paragraph (three to five sentences) about a place in your community that you know well. Start with a sentence that tells the main idea.

scoringGuide.1: A main idea is present but not first, or the support drifts to other ideas.
scoringGuide.2: First sentence states one main idea and at least two later sentences support that same idea.

tasks.fallbackRoute: Before PEEL, teach a paragraph frame (topic sentence + two supporting sentences) with a shared example; the teacher conferences with learners who scored 0 before the write-argument scene.

tasks.prompt: Which sentence is a fact, not an opinion?
tasks.key: Cassava leaves are grown and eaten in many parts of Liberia.
tasks.fallbackRoute: Mini-lesson on the question 'Can it be checked?' with four more classroom sentences before the evidence scene.

tasks.prompt: Should our school have a longer lunch break? Write one reason someone might say yes and one reason someone might say no.

scoringGuide.1: Two reasons on the same side, or one side only.
scoringGuide.2: Two distinct reasons on opposite sides.

tasks.fallbackRoute: Pair talk with the sentence starters 'Some people think … because …' and 'Others think … because …' before the intro scene.

tasks.prompt: Should students be allowed to bring mobile phones to school? Write a thesis statement with your claim and two reasons. Then write one PEEL paragraph that argues your first reason with real evidence, explains it and links it back to your claim (120 to 200 words). Work alone, without hints, the model plan or a partner.
tasks.scoringGuide: Candidate writing rubric: thesis, point, evidence, explain-link (0-2 each, 8 points)

tasks.prompt: Read this paragraph: 'Our school library should open on Saturdays. The library is good because it is good for students. Everyone knows reading is important. If it opens, more students will read.' Name two problems with the reasons or evidence and explain why each one weakens the argument. Then rewrite one sentence so it gives real evidence and says where the evidence comes from.

scoringGuide.1: A problem is named without explanation.
scoringGuide.2: One problem named and explained; rewrite adequate or missing.
scoringGuide.3: Both problems named, one explanation thin, rewrite adequate.
scoringGuide.4: Names circular reasoning (sentence 2) and opinion used as evidence (sentence 3), explains why each fails, and rewrites one with specific, checkable evidence and its source.

tasks.prompt: Claim: 'Every Grade 7 class should plant trees on the school compound.' Write the strongest objection someone could raise, then write two sentences that answer it.

Write a short letter (80 to 150 words) to your town chief or community leader asking for one change at the market, such as lights or a clean water point. Make your claim, give one reason with real evidence, and answer one objection the leader might have.
tasks.scoringGuide: Candidate writing rubric: thesis (as claim), evidence, explain-link, counterargument (0-2 each)
tasks.note: New genre and a real audience: the lesson only rehearses school essays.

tasks.prompt: Without notes: write a thesis statement with two reasons for 'Should every student learn to swim?', then write a PEEL paragraph for one of the reasons.
Choose a question about your school or community. Write a thesis, one PEEL paragraph, one sentence answering an objection, and a two-sentence conclusion that adds no new reason.
tasks.scoringGuide: Candidate writing rubric (8 points) + counterargument (2) + conclusion adds no new reason (0/1)

tasks.prompt: Write a full five-paragraph argumentative essay (introduction, two reasons, one paragraph answering the other side, conclusion) on a question you care about. Then write two sentences explaining which of your reasons is strongest and why.
tasks.scoringGuide: Candidate writing rubric applied per paragraph + counterargument + a reasoned self-evaluation
tasks.note: Optional and non-gating; matches the in-lesson challenge scene. Argumentative essays are MOE Grade 9 scope (grade-scope decision pending).
